draft.title: Errors and limitations
card: Random error
an error that changes from one measurement to the next, sometimes too high and sometimes too low. It scatters results around the true value.
Systematic error
an error that pushes every measurement the same way, such as a balance that always reads 0.5 g too high. It shifts results away from the true value.
Repeating a measurement and averaging helps reduce the effect of random error. It does not remove a systematic error, because every repeat is shifted the same way.
Limitations
Every method has limits, such as the smallest scale division on the equipment, a small sample or conditions that were hard to control. Report them, so readers know how far to trust the results.
draft.remember: Random error scatters results. Systematic error shifts them one way. Report the limits of the method.

a.q: A student heats a sample in a crucible. The balance reads 0.3 g too high every time it is used. What type of error is this?
opts: Systematic error, as every reading is shifted the same way
Random error, as the balance is not reading correctly
Random error, as the readings were taken several times
Systematic error, as the readings are scattered widely
a.why: The balance shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so the error is systematic. It is not random, because random errors vary from one reading to the next and scatter results.
a.clue: Does the error change between readings, or push them all the same way?

b.q: Noah titrates a solution five times and averages his burette readings. Why does averaging NOT fix a burette that was wrongly marked 0.2 mL too low?
opts: Every reading is shifted the same way, so the average is too
Averaging adds more scatter to the results, so error grows
Averaging only works if all the readings are exactly equal
A wrongly marked burette gives random error, so it stays
b.why: A wrongly marked burette is a systematic error, so every reading is shifted by the same amount. The average of shifted readings is still shifted. Averaging helps with random scatter, but it does not remove a shift.
b.clue: Think about what each repeat does to a shift that is the same every time.

a.best: Systematic error, as every reading is shifted the same way

b.best: Every reading is shifted the same way, so the average is too

problems.detail: 'A burette that was wrongly marked 0.2 mL too low' is unclear: it does not say which way the readings are shifted. In a real titration a constant scale offset cancels out when the titre is worked out as final minus initial reading, so the scenario could confuse careful students. A balance or pipette example would be cleaner, or the stem could state the readings are each 0.2 mL off.
